questions.stem: Which functional group is present in every carboxylic acid?
questions.explanation: A carboxylic acid contains the carboxyl group, a carbonyl and a hydroxyl on the same carbon. -CHO is an aldehyde and -COO- joining two carbon chains is an ester.

questions.stem: To which family does CH₃CH₂CHO belong?
questions.explanation: -CHO is a carbonyl group at the end of the chain, which makes this an aldehyde (propanal). In a ketone the carbonyl carbon is bonded to two other carbons.

questions.stem: To which family does CH₃COCH₂CH₃ belong?
questions.explanation: The CO group sits between two carbon atoms, so this is a ketone, butanone. An ester would have the group -COO- with an extra oxygen.

questions.stem: Which compound is an ester?
questions.explanation: In an ester, -COO- links two carbon groups: CH₃CH₂COOCH₃ is methyl propanoate. CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH has the same molecular formula, C₄H₈O₂, but the -COOH group ends the chain, so it is a carboxylic acid.

questions.stem: Which compound is an amide?
questions.explanation: An amide has nitrogen bonded directly to a carbonyl carbon, -CONH₂. CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ is an amine, with no carbonyl, and CH₃CH₂COONH₄ is an ammonium salt of a carboxylic acid.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃?
questions.explanation: The longest chain has four carbons, and numbering from the end nearest the OH group puts it on carbon 2. Numbering from the other end would give the higher locant 3, which is not allowed.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂COOH?
questions.explanation: The carboxyl carbon is always carbon 1. The chain has four carbons including it (butanoic acid), and the methyl branch is on carbon 3. No chain through the carboxyl carbon has five carbons, so a pentanoic acid name miscounts the chain.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: There are five carbons in the chain and the carbonyl is on the middle carbon, carbon 3, from either end. Pentan-2-one has the carbonyl one carbon from the end.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The chain has five carbons, and numbering from the end nearer the double bond gives it the locant 2. Pent-3-ene uses the higher number, so it is not a correct name.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂OH?
questions.explanation: The longest chain containing the OH carbon has four carbons. Numbering starts at the OH end, so the OH is on carbon 1 and the methyl branch is on carbon 3. The functional group gets the lowest number, not the branch.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO?
questions.explanation: There are four carbons including the CHO carbon, so the name is butanal. An aldehyde group is always on carbon 1, so no number is needed.

questions.stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂NH₂?
questions.explanation: The NH₂ group is bonded to a two-carbon chain with no carbonyl, so this is the amine ethanamine. Ethanamide, CH₃CONH₂, has the nitrogen bonded to a carbonyl carbon.

questions.stem: Which is the condensed structural formula of ethanamide?
questions.explanation: Ethanamide has two carbons, one of them a carbonyl carbon bonded to NH₂. CH₃CH₂NH₂ is ethanamine, and CH₃COONH₄ is the salt ammonium ethanoate.

questions.stem: Which formula represents methyl ethanoate?
questions.explanation: Methyl ethanoate comes from methanol and ethanoic acid: the two-carbon acid part, CH₃CO-, keeps the C=O, and the methyl group is joined through the single-bonded oxygen. HCOOCH₂CH₃ is ethyl methanoate, an isomer with the parts reversed.

questions.stem: Ethanol reacts with propanoic acid to form an ester. What is the name of the ester?
questions.explanation: An ester is named with the alcohol part first, as an alkyl group, then the acid part ending in -oate. Ethanol gives 'ethyl' and propanoic acid gives 'propanoate'. Propyl ethanoate would come from propan-1-ol and ethanoic acid.

questions.stem: What are isomers?
options: Compounds with the same structure but different molecular formulae
Atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons
Compounds in one homologous series that differ by CH₂
Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures
questions.explanation: Isomers share a molecular formula but have their atoms arranged differently. Atoms with different numbers of neutrons are isotopes, and members of a homologous series have different formulae.

questions.stem: Which compound is a position isomer of pentan-1-ol?
questions.explanation: Position isomers have the same carbon chain but the functional group in a different place. Pentan-2-ol keeps the straight five-carbon chain with the OH moved to carbon 2. 2-methylbutan-1-ol has a branched chain, so it is a chain isomer.

questions.stem: Which pair are chain isomers?
questions.explanation: Chain isomers differ in the arrangement of the carbon skeleton: butanal has a straight chain and 2-methylpropanal a branched one, both C₄H₈O. Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol are position isomers, and butane and but-1-ene have different formulae.

questions.stem: Which compound has cis and trans isomers?
questions.explanation: Cis-trans isomerism needs a C=C double bond with two different groups on each carbon of the double bond. In but-2-ene each carbon carries H and CH₃. The others each have one double-bond carbon with two identical groups.

questions.stem: Why does but-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃, not have cis and trans isomers?
options: Rotation about its carbon-carbon double bond is completely free
Its double bond is at the end of the chain, so it cannot be named
It has only four carbons, and cis-trans isomers need at least five
One carbon of the double bond carries two identical hydrogen atoms
questions.explanation: Swapping the groups on the CH₂= carbon gives the same molecule, so there are no distinct cis and trans forms. Rotation about a C=C bond is restricted, which is why cis-trans isomers exist at all, and but-2-ene shows them with only four carbons.

questions.stem: These four compounds have similar molar masses. Which list puts them in order of increasing boiling point?
questions.explanation: Butane has only dispersion forces. Propanal adds dipole-dipole forces from its polar C=O. Propan-1-ol forms hydrogen bonds through its O-H. Ethanoic acid has both O-H and C=O, forming especially strong hydrogen bonding, so it boils highest.

questions.stem: Ethanol mixes completely with water, but hexane does not. Why?
options: Ethanol has stronger dispersion forces than hexane has
Ethanol reacts with water to form a new soluble compound
Ethanol forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules; hexane cannot
Ethanol ionises in water to form ions; hexane cannot ionise
questions.explanation: The O-H group of ethanol hydrogen bonds with water, so the two mix. Hexane is non-polar with only dispersion forces, and it cannot replace the hydrogen bonds between water molecules. Ethanol does not ionise appreciably in water.

questions.stem: Why does the solubility of alcohols in water decrease from methanol to octan-1-ol?
options: Larger alcohols ionise less in water, so they form fewer ions in the solution
The longer chains form more hydrogen bonds with each other than with water
The non-polar hydrocarbon chain gets longer while there is still only one OH group
The OH group becomes less polar as the chain gets longer, so it forms no H bonds
questions.explanation: Each alcohol has one OH that can hydrogen bond with water, but the growing non-polar chain can only form dispersion forces and disrupts the water's hydrogen bonding. The OH group stays polar, but it is a smaller part of a larger molecule.

questions.stem: Methyl ethanoate (M = 74) boils at 57 °C, but propanoic acid (M = 74) boils at 141 °C. Which explanation is correct?
options: The acid has a longer carbon chain, so its dispersion forces are much stronger
The ester has no O-H group, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other
The ester has no C=O group, so its molecules have only weak dispersion forces
The ester is non-polar, so its molecules are held only by dispersion forces
questions.explanation: Both molecules have a polar C=O and similar dispersion forces, but only the acid has an O-H group, so only it forms hydrogen bonds between molecules. The ester is polar and has dipole-dipole forces, just no hydrogen bonding between its own molecules.

questions.stem: Propanone, CH₃COCH₃, is fully miscible with water even though it has no O-H group. Why?
options: Propanone ionises completely in water to form small ions
Its carbon chain is short enough to hydrogen bond with water
Its C-H bonds are polar enough to hydrogen bond with water
Water molecules hydrogen bond to the oxygen of its C=O group
questions.explanation: The carbonyl oxygen carries a partial negative charge and lone pairs, so it can accept hydrogen bonds from water's O-H groups. C-H bonds are not polar enough to take part in hydrogen bonding.

questions.stem: What is the main organic product when propan-1-ol is refluxed with excess acidified potassium dichromate solution?
questions.explanation: A primary alcohol is oxidised first to an aldehyde, and with excess oxidant under reflux the aldehyde is oxidised further to the carboxylic acid. Propanone would come from the secondary alcohol, propan-2-ol.

questions.stem: Butan-2-ol is warmed with acidified potassium permanganate. What is the organic product, and what is observed?
options: Butanoic acid; the orange solution becomes green
Butanone; the colourless solution becomes purple
Butanone; the purple solution becomes colourless
Butanal; the purple solution becomes colourless
questions.explanation: A secondary alcohol is oxidised to a ketone, here butanone, and the purple MnO₄⁻ is reduced to almost colourless Mn²⁺. An orange to green change is seen with dichromate, not permanganate.

questions.stem: 2-methylpropan-2-ol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate. What is observed?
options: The solution turns green, because a ketone forms from the tertiary alcohol
The solution turns green, because a carboxylic acid forms as the product
The solution turns purple, because the dichromate is reduced to Cr³⁺
The solution stays orange, because a tertiary alcohol is not oxidised
questions.explanation: In a tertiary alcohol, the carbon bearing the OH has no hydrogen atom, so it cannot be oxidised by dichromate. The orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ remains. Reduction to Cr³⁺ would turn the solution green, not purple.

questions.stem: Which test distinguishes propanal from propanone?
options: Add bromine water: propanone decolourises it, while propanal leaves it orange
Warm with acidified dichromate: propanal turns it green, propanone leaves it orange
Warm with acidified dichromate: propanone turns it green, propanal leaves it orange
Add sodium carbonate: propanal fizzes, while propanone gives no bubbles
questions.explanation: Aldehydes are readily oxidised to carboxylic acids, so propanal reduces orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ to green Cr³⁺. Ketones resist oxidation, so propanone gives no change. Neither compound is acidic enough to fizz with a carbonate.

questions.stem: Which observation shows that a compound is a carboxylic acid?
options: It fizzes with sodium carbonate solution, giving carbon dioxide
It decolourises bromine water rapidly at room temperature
It turns acidified dichromate from orange to green on warming
It forms an ester when warmed with sodium chloride solution
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids are weak acids, so they react with carbonates: 2RCOOH + CO₃²⁻ → 2RCOO⁻ + H₂O + CO₂. Decolourising bromine water shows an alkene, and turning dichromate green shows a primary or secondary alcohol or an aldehyde.

questions.stem: Which reagent distinguishes hex-1-ene from hexan-1-ol?
options: Bromine water, which only hex-1-ene decolourises quickly
Acidified permanganate, which only hexan-1-ol decolourises
Sodium carbonate solution, which fizzes with hexan-1-ol
Acidified dichromate, which only hex-1-ene turns green
questions.explanation: Bromine adds rapidly across the C=C bond of hex-1-ene, removing the orange colour, while hexan-1-ol does not react. Acidified permanganate oxidises both compounds, so it cannot tell them apart, and an alcohol is not acidic enough to react with carbonate.

questions.stem: But-2-ene reacts with water in the presence of an acid catalyst. What is the product?
questions.explanation: Water adds across the double bond, H to one carbon and OH to the other. Because but-2-ene is symmetrical, the OH ends up on carbon 2 whichever way it adds. This addition is not an oxidation, so no ketone forms.

questions.stem: Which equation shows the reaction of ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide solution?
questions.explanation: Ethanoic acid is monoprotic: its carboxyl hydrogen is transferred to OH⁻, forming water and the salt sodium ethanoate. This acid-base reaction is used to identify carboxylic acids.

questions.stem: Ethanol is heated with ethanoic acid and a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid. What is the main role of the sulfuric acid?
options: It acts as a catalyst for the esterification
It oxidises the ethanol to ethanoic acid first
It provides the oxygen atom found in the ester
It neutralises the ethanoic acid to form a salt
questions.explanation: Concentrated sulfuric acid catalyses the condensation of the acid and alcohol to ethyl ethanoate and water; it also absorbs some of the water formed. It does not oxidise ethanol here or become part of the ester.

questions.stem: Which is the balanced equation for the complete combustion of ethanol?
questions.explanation: Two carbons give 2CO₂ and six hydrogens give 3H₂O, which contain 7 O atoms. Ethanol supplies one, so 6 O atoms, or 3O₂, are needed. Forgetting the oxygen in ethanol gives 3½O₂.

questions.stem: Which ester forms when methanol reacts with butanoic acid?
questions.explanation: The acid's carbonyl stays with its own chain, CH₃CH₂CH₂CO-, and the methanol supplies the -OCH₃ group, giving methyl butanoate. The second formula is propyl ethanoate, an isomer made from propan-1-ol and ethanoic acid.

questions.stem: Use C = 12.01, H = 1.008, O = 16.00. A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. What is its empirical formula?
questions.explanation: Moles per 100 g: C 40.0/12.01 = 3.33, H 6.7/1.008 = 6.6, O 53.3/16.00 = 3.33. Dividing by 3.33 gives 1 : 2 : 1, so the empirical formula is CH₂O.

questions.stem: A compound has the empirical formula C₂H₄O and a molar mass of 88 g mol⁻¹. It fizzes with sodium carbonate. What is its molecular formula, and which compound could it be?
questions.explanation: C₂H₄O has M = 44, so the molecular formula is double: C₄H₈O₂. Both butanoic acid and ethyl ethanoate fit that formula, but only a carboxylic acid fizzes with carbonate.

questions.stem: Use C = 12.01, H = 1.008, O = 16.00. Complete combustion of 0.440 g of a compound of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen gives 0.880 g of CO₂ and 0.360 g of H₂O. What is its empirical formula?
Compound X, C₃H₈O, is oxidised by acidified dichromate to compound Y. Y does not react with sodium carbonate and is not oxidised further by dichromate. What is X?
questions.explanation: Y resists further oxidation and is not acidic, so it is a ketone, propanone. Ketones come from secondary alcohols, so X is propan-2-ol. Propan-1-ol would give propanal and then propanoic acid, which fizzes with carbonate.
